At 11:40 p.m., the last ferry pulls away from Slip 3, churning the harbor water into a brief, pale froth before the dark folds back over it. From the window of the Lost Property office, you can watch its stern light shrink until it blurs with the buoys along the breakwater. Then the automatic doors lock with a pneumatic sigh, the vending machine down the concourse clicks into its louder midnight hum, and the terminal belongs entirely to the mop buckets and me.

People imagine that a lost-and-found room smells of dust, like an attic. In truth, ours smells of damp wool, cheap citrus disinfectant, and brine. Everything left on a boat carries the sea in its fibers for at least a week. By the time a forgotten coat dries out on our cedar hangers, its owner has usually decided they didn't like the fit anyway, or bought a replacement in a town forty miles inland, or simply accepted the loss as part of the general tax of moving from one place to another.

Most of what comes across my counter is predictable. There is an entire drawer dedicated to single gloves—always the left hand, for some reason I have never bothered to investigate—and a tall plastic bin bristling with black umbrellas whose ribs have surrendered to the wind off the sound. There are phone chargers coiled like small gray snakes, paperback thrillers swollen to twice their thickness by mist, and plastic sunglasses with one temple held on by a twist of silver wire. We log each item in a wide green ledger with columns for *Date*, *Vessel*, *Description*, and *Disposition*. After ninety days, "Disposition" almost always turns into a single word: *Donated*, *Discarded*, or, in the rare case of keys, *Scrap*.

There is a strange intimacy to sorting through what people drop when they are late. You learn that nobody rushes gracefully. When the whistle blows for final boarding, dignity is the first luggage thrown overboard. A woman leaves her silk scarf tangled around a bench slat; a man leaves a brown paper bag containing two bruised pears and a receipt from a hardware store in Port Townsend; a child leaves a plastic dinosaur tucked neatly into the gap between two bolted seats, perhaps as a sentry, perhaps because the tide of distraction simply carried them up the gangplank without it.

Tonight’s haul was light—just a canvas tote filled with library books due three Tuesdays ago, a thermos still warm enough to steam when I cracked the lid, and a small cardboard box bound with faded blue butcher’s twine. Deckhand Miller dropped them off on his way to the parking lot, his yellow slicker dripping a neat trail across my linoleum. "Found the box under the life-vest locker on the *Kestrel*," he said, already yawning. "No name on it. Thought it might be someone’s lunch, till I shook it."

I waited until the terminal was quiet before untying the knot. Inside, wrapped in a page torn from last summer’s maritime almanac, was a wooden flute—not the silver kind you see in school bands, all keys and bright machinery, but a plain, dark tube of turned rosewood with six finger holes worn smooth at the edges. Beside it lay a crumpled piece of waxed paper holding three dried bay leaves and a brass tuning slide stained green with verdigris. No phone number. No monogram. Just the faint, sweet scent of cedar oil and old breath.

I set it on the blotter under my desk lamp. Objects like this are the hardest ones to file. A wallet is easy; it practically shouts its owner's name, begging to be reunited with a driver's license and a stack of laminated punch cards. Even a coat wants a pair of shoulders. But a handmade thing without a tag feels like it belongs to a story I walked into halfway through the third act. Had someone carried it out onto the upper deck to play while the fog rolled in, only to tuck it under the bench when the deckhands started hosing down the rails? Or had they left it there on purpose, tired of carrying a small regret across the water?

I have worked the night desk for six winters, and I have learned not to invent too much. Imagination is good company at two in the morning, but it makes for poor recordkeeping. Still, you cannot hold a worn piece of wood under a lamp without wondering about the hands that shaped the smoothness around the lower holes—whether they were steady or quick, calloused from rope or ink-stained from a desk like mine.

At 1:15, I wrote *Flute, wooden, dark finish, w/ box and leaves* on line 412 of the ledger. I tied a manila tag around the upper joint, careful not to pull the string too tight against the grain, and placed the box on Shelf C, between a ceramic mug painted with lighthouses and a leatherette Bible whose spine had cracked down the middle of Psalms.

Outside, the harbor fog was thickening, softening the sodium streetlights along the pier into blurred amber moons. Somewhere beyond the pilings, a bell buoy tolled once, twice, rocked by the swell of an unseen freighter passing out in the shipping lane. Most things that come to Shelf C stay until their ninety days are up. Every now and then, though, the door opens at 6:00 a.m. before my shift ends, and someone steps in breathless, cheeks red from running down the ramp, asking if by any miracle anyone turned in a small box tied with blue string. And on those mornings, handing it back across the scratched Formica feels less like clerk work and more like returning a piece of the world to its proper weight.
